metaDescription: Obstacles, soil load, furniture moves, and security escorts can raise VCT strip and wax quotes 15%-45%. See the math, then compare bids side by side.
excerpt: VCT strip and wax quotes swing 15 to 45 percent above the national $0.30 to $0.60 per sq ft baseline because of site conditions, not vendor greed. Learn which five factors drive the premium and how to reduce each one before the crew arrives.
quickAnswer: A clean, open VCT floor typically strips and refinishes for $0.30 to $0.45 per sq ft nationally. Dense furniture and obstacles add 10 to 20 percent, heavy soil load or 6+ layers of old finish adds 10 to 25 percent, and after-hours security escorts, elevator restrictions, or weekend-only access can push the total 15 to 45 percent above baseline, often landing at $0.50 to $0.75 per sq ft.

blocks.text: How Vendors Build a Strip and Wax Estimate

Floor care contractors start with production rates. A two-person crew on an open, empty VCT floor can strip, rinse, and apply five coats of finish to roughly 2,000 to 3,000 sq ft in an eight-hour shift. At specialty labor rates of $55 to $95 per technician hour plus chemistry, pads, and equipment wear, that produces the national baseline of about $0.30 to $0.45 per sq ft for straightforward jobs. Every site condition that slows the crew lowers production and raises the per-sq-ft price, because the vendor still has to cover the same crew-hours.

Understanding this production logic lets an office manager predict a quote before the walkthrough and, more importantly, remove the conditions that inflate it. Below are the five site factors estimators weigh most heavily, ranked by how often they move the final number.

Open corridors are fast. A cubicle farm with VCT under every workstation is slow. Each desk, mobile pedestal, and chair must be moved off the area, then returned after the final coat cures, which is typically 30 to 60 minutes between coats and several hours before furniture can return. Estimators often count workstations and add 5 to 10 minutes of handling per station, twice. For a 4,000 sq ft area with 40 workstations, that can add 8 to 13 labor hours, or $440 to $1,200 at specialty rates.

Fixed obstacles matter too: casework, built-in reception desks, and columns create edges that must be detailed by hand with scour pads. High edge-to-area ratios, common in small private offices, increase hand-work time significantly.
Factor 2: Soil Load and Finish Buildup

Soil load describes how much embedded dirt, old finish, and contamination sits on the tile. A floor that was last stripped two years ago with regular burnishing may need one stripper pass. A floor with eight to twelve layers of yellowed finish, ground-in grit near entrances, or residue from incompatible cleaners can need two or three passes with longer dwell times, aggressive black pads, and more rinse water. Using an incompatible high-alkaline daily cleaner instead of a neutral-pH product, for example a 1:64 dilution neutral concentrate, accelerates finish breakdown and haze, which shows up as soil load at strip time.

blocks.text: Factor 3: After-Hours Security Escorts and Access Rules

Many Class A buildings require contractors to be escorted by building security, sign in at a loading dock, or work only between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. on weekends. Some landlords charge the tenant for escort time directly, often $35 to $65 per hour. Vendors also price in night or weekend differentials for their crews. If the escort arrives late or the freight elevator is locked, crew time is wasted and the vendor bakes that risk into the bid.

blocks.title: Ask the property manager before the walkthrough
blocks.text: Get written building rules covering contractor hours, escort fees, elevator reservations, and noise limits before the vendor estimates. Sharing those rules upfront prevents change orders and lets every bidder price the same conditions.

Stripping uses a lot of solution and rinse water, and the slurry must be recovered and disposed of properly rather than poured into storm drains. A janitor closet with a mop sink on the same floor keeps the job efficient. If crews must haul buckets to a distant service sink or ride elevators with wet vacuums, production drops. Upper floors without freight elevators and multi-tenant floors with shared corridors add setup time and coning requirements.
Factor 5: Cure Time and Reopening Deadlines

A quality finish such as a 25 percent solids zinc-interlocked acrylic needs time between coats and a longer cure before traffic. If the office must reopen by 7 a.m. on Monday, the vendor may add air movers, extra technicians, or split the job across two nights. Each option adds cost. Allowing a full weekend window is one of the easiest ways to bring a quote back toward baseline.
How to Cut the Premium Before the Crew Arrives

items.name: Clear the floor yourself
items.text: Have staff relocate personal items, under-desk boxes, and small furniture the afternoon before. Ask the vendor to price the job with and without furniture moving.

items.name: Control soil load between strips
items.text: Use entrance matting, daily dust mopping, and neutral-pH damp mopping. Schedule scrub-and-recoat two to four times a year so the annual strip needs only one pass.

items.name: Pre-arrange building access
items.text: Reserve the freight elevator, confirm escort coverage, and give the vendor badge access in writing.

items.name: Offer a full weekend
items.text: A Friday night to Sunday window lets coats cure naturally and reduces crew size.

items.name: Bid the job with a clear spec
items.text: List VCT square footage, finish coat count, and access rules so bids reflect the same conditions.

blocks.title: Safety and documentation still apply
blocks.text: Regardless of price pressure, require a certificate of insurance, Safety Data Sheets for stripper and finish under OSHA HazCom, and proper coning of closed areas. Restroom-adjacent VCT may also involve bloodborne pathogen precautions if contamination is present.

Small convenience upgrades also help after the job: a compact touchless towel dispenser in the kitchenette reduces drips and wet foot traffic onto freshly finished tile, which protects gloss between maintenance visits.

faqs.q: Why did my VCT strip and wax quote come in 40 percent higher than the national average?
faqs.a: Stacked site factors are the usual reason. Dense furniture, heavy finish buildup, weekend-only access with security escorts, and a hard reopening deadline each add 5 to 25 percent. Combined, they can push a $0.38 per sq ft baseline to $0.51 to $0.55. Ask the vendor to itemize each premium so you can address the ones you control.

faqs.q: Does moving furniture count as a separate charge?
faqs.a: Often yes. Many contracts list furniture moving as an exclusion or price it per workstation or per labor hour at $55 to $95. Light items like chairs and wastebaskets are commonly included, while desks, filing cabinets, and casework are quoted separately. Get the treatment in writing before the job date.

faqs.q: How does soil load affect the number of stripper passes?
faqs.a: Floors with one to three layers of finish and regular maintenance usually strip in a single pass. Floors with six or more layers, yellowed edges, or residue from incompatible cleaners may need two or three passes with longer chemical dwell times, which can add 10 to 25 percent to the labor and chemical cost.

faqs.q: Can I lower the price by scheduling more frequent scrub-and-recoat visits?
faqs.a: Usually. Scrub-and-recoat removes the top finish layers and soil without full stripping, which keeps buildup low. Offices that recoat two to four times a year often stretch full strips to every 18 to 24 months and see lower strip pricing because the floor needs fewer passes. Over a year, using 4.333 weeks per month in your frequency math, total floor spend often drops.

faqs.q: What insurance and compliance items should I confirm for after-hours floor work?
faqs.a: Confirm a current certificate of insurance naming your company and landlord as additional insured, workers compensation coverage, Safety Data Sheets for all chemicals under OSHA Hazard Communication, and any building-specific contractor rules. Ask whether the finish is Green Seal certified if you track sustainability metrics.
